October 26, 2026 · Multi-Agent Harness² · Research note

Can an AI research team improve how it works?

Multi-Agent Harness² explores how scientific agents can revise their procedures and information handoffs—with frozen model weights—and what prevents those revisions from becoming reliable improvements.

An AI research team can have a planner, a coder, and a verifier—and still fail because the right information never reaches the right agent.

A verifier might discover an error that never gets back to the planner. A coder might receive an analysis plan without the data dimensions needed to implement it correctly. Each agent can appear competent while the team’s workflow breaks down.

This raises a practical question: can an agent team improve its own way of working while it solves a scientific task?

Our study, Multi-Agent Harness²: Recursive Revision of Scientific Agent Teams, investigates that question. Building on Harness², we let a team revise its execution procedures, test proposed changes, and retain runnable solutions together with the workflows that produced them.

The model weights stay frozen. What changes is how the team works.

Two places a workflow can go wrong

We distinguish between two kinds of revision.

Role revisions change how an individual agent performs its job. A coding agent, for example, might receive better instructions for inspecting an array before building a predictor.

Coordination revisions change what agents communicate and how information moves between them. A planner might be required to pass observed array dimensions to the coder, rather than leaving the coder to infer them.

These interventions address different problems. Separating them makes the proposed changes easier to inspect, execute, and compare.

It also makes failures more informative: did the team need a better procedure, a better handoff, or better evidence for deciding which revision to keep?

From a proposed improvement to an executed test

Multi-Agent Harness² runs a bounded revision cycle:

  1. Execute the current workflow to establish a reference solution.
  2. Propose role and coordination changes separately.
  3. Run candidate workflows and collect evidence from their execution.
  4. Compose a candidate using the tested evidence.
  5. Select and retain a runnable program and its generating workflow.
  6. Carry the selected state into the next round.

The process runs for up to three recursive rounds per task. Each new task starts with a reset workflow, lessons, and archive.

The optimizer uses the task information and execution evidence available to it. Official benchmark feedback is withheld until the final program has been committed.

This boundary matters: the team must decide what to keep without repeatedly consulting the final grader.

What happened on scientific programming tasks?

We evaluated the system on all 38 machine-graded ScienceAgentBench tasks.

Results on the complete 38-task evaluation
MethodTasks solvedSuccess rate
Base GLM team11 / 3828.9%
MASS-RHI workflow search11 / 3828.9%
GLM Multi-Agent Harness²13 / 3834.2%

The aggregate improvement is two tasks, or 5.3 percentage points. But the paired comparison with MASS is statistically inconclusive: p = 0.754.

Looking at individual tasks explains why the headline alone is insufficient. Multi-Agent Harness² solves six tasks that MASS misses, while MASS solves four that Multi-Agent Harness² misses. The revision process produces gains and regressions.

It also costs more in realized GLM API expenditure: $19.18, compared with $13.35 for MASS and $0.68 for the base team across the 38 tasks. These figures exclude calibration and scientific compute.

The experiment therefore does not establish general superiority or better performance per dollar.

The biggest bottleneck: deciding what to keep

The execution traces reveal a striking gap between generating a revision and retaining it.

Across 114 entered rounds, the all-GLM system produces:

  • 38 valid changed coordination proposals;
  • 11 rounds in which composition adopts changed coordination;
  • 1 round in which final selection retains a coordination change.

These stages are not a simple funnel: selection can retain a candidate that composition rejected. Nevertheless, the gap is substantial.

Many selection decisions fail to complete the required evidence protocol. Some lack an executed structured check; others reach tool or input-reading limits.

This suggests a concrete engineering priority: better proposals need to be accompanied by checks that can distinguish useful changes and support a valid selection decision.

One repair that changed the scientific result

A retrospective analysis of the hybrid system provides a tangible example.

On an EEG prediction task, a selected coordination candidate changes the predictor from 17 channel features to 3,400 channel–time features, alongside changes to standardization and regularization.

The official Spearman score rises from 0.0558 to 0.6384, crossing the task’s 0.6 success threshold.

That is an observed scientific repair. Because several changes occur together, it does not isolate the effect of the coordination contract alone.

Other successful tasks retain their initial programs across every revision round. Those cases make another distinction essential: a successful final answer is not automatically evidence of successful recursive improvement.

What the hybrid experiment tells us

We also explored a hybrid configuration using Codex for coordination revisions and GLM for the other components.

It solves 14 of 35 completed tasks, compared with 9 for MASS on those same tasks. However, the run stopped for resource reasons, and Codex adds computation outside the GLM budget.

The result is exploratory. It should not be compared directly with the complete 38-task totals or treated as proof that a stronger coordinator caused the difference.

Toward agent teams that improve reliably

Multi-Agent Harness² provides an inspectable way to study workflow revision: what was proposed, what was executed, what was retained, and whether the resulting program actually improved.

The next challenge is making that loop more dependable. Execution checks must capture scientific correctness, selection must preserve useful changes, and evaluation must separate genuine improvement from additional computation and stochastic variation.

An agent team’s ability to suggest a change is only the beginning. The harder question is whether it can produce the evidence needed to keep the right one.

Based on the manuscript Multi-Agent Harness²: Recursive Revision of Scientific Agent Teams. Results reflect the manuscript version discussed here. The conceptual illustration was created for this article.
